evidence.excerpt:
We present some updates to YOLO! We made a bunch
of little design changes to make it better . We also trained
this new network that's pretty swell. It's a little bigger than
last time but more accurate. It's still fast though, don't
worry. At 320 × 320 YOLOv3 runs in 22 ms at 28.2 mAP ,
as accurate as SSD but three times faster . When we look
at the old .5 IOU mAP detection metric YOLOv3 is quite
good. It achieves 57.9 AP50 in 51 ms on a Titan X, com-
pared to 57.5 AP50 in 198 ms by RetinaNet, similar perfor-
mance but 3.8 × faster . As always, all the code is online at
https://pjreddie.com/yolo/.

Following YOLO9000 our system predicts bounding
boxes using dimension clusters as anchor boxes [15]. The
network predicts 4 coordinates for each bounding box, tx,
ty,tw,th. If the cell is offset from the top left corner of the
image by (cx,c y) and the bounding box prior has width and
heightpw,ph, then the predictions correspond to:
bx =σ(tx) +cx
by =σ(ty) +cy
bw =pwetw
bh =pheth
During training we use sum of squared error loss. If the
ground truth for some coordinate prediction is ˆt* our gra-
dient is the ground truth value (computed from the ground
truth box) minus our prediction: ˆt* −t*. This ground truth
value can be easily computed by inverting the equations
above.
YOLOv3 predicts an objectness score for each bounding
box using logistic regression. This should be 1 if the bound-
ing box prior overlaps a ground truth object by more than
any other bounding box prior. If the

evidence.excerpt:
Each box predicts the classes the bounding box may con-
tain using multilabel classification. We do not use a softmax
as we have found it is unnecessary for good performance,
instead we simply use independent logistic classifiers. Dur-
ing training we use binary cross-entropy loss for the class
predictions.
This formulation helps when we move to more complex
domains like the Open Images Dataset [7]. In this dataset
there are many overlapping labels (i.e. Woman and Person).
Using a softmax imposes the assumption that each box has
exactly one class which is often not the case. A multilabel
approach better models the data.

cept to feature pyramid networks [8]. From our base fea-
ture extractor we add several convolutional layers. The last
of these predicts a 3-d tensor encoding bounding box, ob-
jectness, and class predictions. In our experiments with
COCO [10] we predict 3 boxes at each scale so the tensor is
N ×N × [3 ∗ (4 + 1 + 80)] for the 4 bounding box offsets,
1 objectness prediction, and 80 class predictions.

upsample it by 2×. We also take a feature map from earlier

Table 1. Darknet-53.
This new network is much more powerful than Darknet-
19 but still more efficient than ResNet-101 or ResNet-152.
Here are some ImageNet results:
Backbone Top-1 Top-5 Bn Ops BFLOP/s FPS
Darknet-19 [15] 74.1 91.8 7.29 1246 171
ResNet-101[5] 77.1 93.7 19.7 1039 53
ResNet-152 [5] 77.6 93.8 29.4 1090 37
Darknet-53 77.2 93.8 18.7 1457 78
Table 2. Comparison of backbones. Accuracy, billions of oper-
ations, billion floating point operations per second, and FPS for
various networks.
Each network is trained with identical settings and tested
at 256 × 256, single crop accuracy. Run times are measured
on a Titan X at 256 × 256. Thus Darknet-53 performs on
par with state-of-the-art classifiers but with fewer floating
point operations and more speed.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Reported gains are measured against established COCO and ImageNet benchmark metrics, with comparison tables adapted from prior external work.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Headline outcomes are reported on standard external benchmarks: COCO mAP/AP50/AP75 and ImageNet top-1/top-5 accuracy.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The system is trained with sum of squared error for box coordinates and binary cross-entropy for objectness and class predictions on ground-truth annotated data.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding superior runtime speed and competitive AP50 accuracy compared to one-stage and two-stage detectors are directly supported by benchmark tables and timing data, with transparent reporting of lower performance at higher IoU thresholds (AP75) and on medium-to-large objects.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The model is evaluated on standard object detection benchmarks (COCO mAP at multiple IoU thresholds) and classification benchmarks (ImageNet), providing standardized comparisons of speed and accuracy trade-offs against relevant baselines such as SSD, RetinaNet, and Faster R-CNN.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Empirical validation was performed using standard MS COCO test-dev evaluations and benchmark comparison tables adapted from external prior work.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard COCO evaluation server/benchmark metrics (mAP, AP50, AP75) and ImageNet top-1/top-5 classification accuracy.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Standard multi-task loss functions (sum of squared error for coordinates, binary cross-entropy for class and objectness predictions) trained on ground-truth annotated training sets.

primary.limitations: The report explicitly acknowledges weaknesses, such as lagging behind state-of-the-art detectors under stricter IoU criteria and failing to improve performance with focal loss or linear coordinate predictions.
primary.method_assessment: The architecture and design adaptations are clearly detailed, including the Darknet-53 layer specifications, anchor clustering details, bounding box parameterizations, and training losses.
primary.quality_rationale: Despite an informal tech-report tone, the paper presents a concrete, well-specified architectural contribution with rigorous empirical benchmarking on standard computer vision datasets.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces YOLOv3, an incremental update to the YOLO real-time object detection framework incorporating a 53-layer residual backbone (Darknet-53), multi-scale feature pyramid-like prediction across three scales, and independent logistic classifiers for multilabel classification.

scholarly_quality.rationale: Despite an informal tech-report tone, the paper presents a concrete, well-specified architectural contribution with rigorous empirical benchmarking on standard computer vision datasets.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The report explicitly acknowledges weaknesses, such as lagging behind state-of-the-art detectors under stricter IoU criteria and failing to improve performance with focal loss or linear coordinate predictions.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.

relation_to_agentic_memory.value: Directly concerns the YOLO family or real-time single-stage detection

research_relevance.value: Foundational anchor: YOLOv3, the iteration most later YOLO work is measured against.
